div.para: \(50 + 1 + 12 = 51 + 12\), or \(63 = 63\) (or equivalent). Yes, it is still a true equation.

problem.para: Perform each of the following operations and answer these questions: What does each resulting equation look like? Is it still a true equation?
1. Add 12 to each side of the equation.

div.para: \(50 + 1 + 10 + 2 = 51 + 12\), or \(63 = 63\) (or equivalent). Yes, it is still a true equation.

exercise.problem: 2. Add \(10 + 2\) to the left side of the equation and 12 to the right side.

div.para: \(50 + 1 + 4 + 3 = 51 + 7\), or \(58 = 58\) (or equivalent). Yes, it is still a true equation.

para.span: 3. Add the equation \(4 + 3 = 7\) to the equation \(50 + 1 = 51\).

div.para: Your answer may vary, but here are some samples.

list.item: \(a + a = 2a\). Added to the original equation gives: \(50 + 1 + a + a = 51 + 2a\), or \(51 + 2a = 51 + 2a\).

para.span: 4. Write a new equation that, when added to \(50 + 1 = 51\), gives a sum that is also a true equation.

div.para: Your answer may vary, but here are some samples

list.item: \(3 + 2 = 7\). Added to the original equation gives: \(50 + 1 + 3 + 2 = 51 + 7\), or \(56 = 58\), which is false.
\(a + 2 = a\). Added to the original equation gives: \(50 + 1 + a + 2 = 51 + a\), or \(53 + a = 51 + a\), which is false.

para.span: 5. Write a new equation that, when added to \(50 + 1 = 51\), gives a sum that is a false equation.
